critique.good: Field column at 147px is the only one that works: account_email, postal_code_us, currency_amount and eu_vat_id all stay whole, and the row key is a stable left anchor. Total width respects the 360px box.
critique.problems: Unreadable as a reference sheet. The Pattern column collapses to 2–3 characters per line, so the regex is shattered into 24–34 line vertical ribbons; the Example column shows 'mira…or' stacked letter by letter and the Error column is a one-word-per-line column of prose. 82 mid-word splits means identifiers, atoms and quantifiers are cut mid-token — exactly the content the table exists to protect. 3523px of scrolling for 7 rows.
critique.cause: Widths [147,100,55,57] spend half the budget on Field, which needs only 126px of content, and starve the three columns that carry the actual data. Pattern needs ~1074px one-line and got 100; Example needs 167px for its longest token and got 55; Error prose needs ~180px to read and got 57. Squeezing to fit the box is the wrong decision here because the widest column is 10× the box.

critique.good: Trades width from Field to Pattern (120→145), which is the right instinct, and keeps the Field column readable enough that most identifiers survive.
critique.problems: Worse than r0A overall: 4453px tall, 129 mid-word splits, and now Field itself starts breaking (account_em / ail, effective_dat / e, currency_am / ount) so the lookup handle is destroyed too. The Example column at 45px is a vertical letter column; headers wrap into fragments ('Exa mple vali d').
critique.cause: The extra 45px given to Pattern is meaningless against a 1074px requirement, while the 27px taken from Field and the reduction of Example to 45 and Error to 49 push those columns below the width of a single word. Redistribution inside a 359px total cannot work at all — the budget is the problem, not the split.

critique.good: The only design that is legible as a table: headers unwrapped (0/4 wrapped), rows read as units at 106–153px, regex breaks at | and ( boundaries instead of inside character classes, only 3 mid-word splits, 919px total height. Column proportions are broadly right — Field 150 anchors the row, Pattern is clearly the dominant column, Example and Error are secondary.
critique.problems: Overflows the 360px box by 561px, so on the phone viewport the reader sees only Field and Pattern and must scroll past the fold to reach the example and the error copy — the row stops being a unit at the moment of reading. Example at 120px still splits the 167px token (the 3 mid-word splits) and wraps values to 3 lines; Error at 170px is just under the 178px the 'Error message' header needs, so that header wraps while the others do not, breaking header symmetry.
critique.cause: Total 921px is set by Pattern 480 (a good choice, it produces the fewest regex lines) but the remaining 441px is misallocated: Example is 47px short of its longest unbreakable token, Error is 8px short of its header, and Field is 3px over the 147px it actually needs.

critique.good: Field column sits at its 147px minimum so every identifier (account_email, postal_code_us) stays on one unbroken line and acts as a reliable row anchor. The Pattern column at 415px is wide enough that most regexes land in 3–4 lines, so the row rhythm is fairly even and the alternation groups in the email rule mostly hold together.
critique.problems: The email regex suffers one mid-word split: a character class / quantifier region is cut across lines, so a reader copying the pattern can no longer tell whether the break is part of the rule. Example valid (185px) and Error message (180px) are far below their one-line widths (264 / 700), so the spec pair would wrap into 2–3 lines each and the error copy into 5+ lines, inflating rows that are currently only tall because of Pattern. Row heights jump 106 → 153 → 83, which breaks vertical rhythm and makes the table look ragged. And despite all that compression the table still overflows by 568px, so the reader pays the full cost of horizontal scrolling without getting an intact regex.
critique.cause: Pattern 415px is just under the width the long alternation groups need (r1C shows 470px clears the splits), while Example 185 and Error 180 are squeezed to near their minimum unbreakable widths — the budget was spent on a still-inadequate Pattern and starved the two right-hand columns.

critique.good: The narrowest total (848px) of the three, so the least horizontal scrolling, and the Field column is again exactly at its unbreakable minimum. Every row starts cleanly with an intact identifier, so the lookup handle survives even in a squeezed layout.
critique.problems: Worst regex rendering of the set: the email pattern fragments into six lines with two mid-word splits, cutting through braces and parenthesised groups so the rule becomes unreadable and un-copyable. Rows inflate to 153px and the table grows to 919px tall — taller than both wider designs — so the narrower table actually costs more vertical scrolling. The 340px Pattern is visibly cramped next to the 185px Example, an inversion of importance.
critique.cause: Pattern 340px is below the width needed to break only at | ( [ { boundaries; the reader loses on both axes at once — no width saving in height, and splits on top of it.

critique.good: The only design with zero mid-word splits: at 470px the email regex breaks cleanly between alternation branches and character-class groups, so patterns remain legible and safe to copy. Field stays intact at 147px, and the Pattern column finally carries its weight as the densest, most-consulted content.
critique.problems: It is the widest table (986px, 626px overflow) and the extra width buys nothing on the right: Example valid at 188px is exactly its 167px longest-word minimum, so sample values still wrap to two lines and the 'rule + valid sample' pair can never be read on one line together. Error message at 180px wraps the prose into four-plus lines. Rows stay 106–153px tall because the regex still needs 5–6 lines, so the table is simultaneously very wide and very tall.
critique.cause: Pattern 470 was set by the split threshold and everything else was fitted to the leftover budget; Example and Error are under-allocated relative to their content, so width is spent where it already works and withheld where cells are actually breaking.

critique.good: The regex column is the most readable of the three: at 560px the long account_email rule breaks at group boundaries (`(?:\.[A-Za-z0-9])?` starts a new line) into 4 clean fragments, and the Field column sits exactly at its 147px no-split minimum so identifiers stay whole.
critique.problems: Worst overflow of the three (1086px, 726px past the box), so Example valid and Error message are both entirely off-screen at 360px and no row can be read as a unit — the reader sees a field name and a wall of regex and nothing else. Worse, it buys nothing: the tallest cell is still 6 lines, one line *taller* than r2B which is 58px narrower. Row 4 (effective_date) is 153px tall although its regex fits on one line at this width.
critique.cause: Pattern is given 560px — about 90px past the point where the regex stops being the binding constraint. Once a row's height is set by the Error/Example columns (190/188, near their floors), extra pattern width converts 1:1 into scroll cost and zero legibility gain. The width budget is being spent on the column that already fits.

critique.good: The strongest of the three: shortest table (779px) and the lowest tallest-cell (5 lines), because 470px is right at the threshold where most patterns fall into 2–3 structure-respecting lines, and the prose columns at 215/195 are generous enough to keep error copy to 4 lines. No mid-word splits anywhere.
critique.problems: Still 668px of overflow, so the two right-hand columns — the ones that tell you whether the rule works and what the user sees when it doesn't — are invisible on arrival. The Example valid column is over-provisioned: 215px for content whose one-line width is 264 and whose longest word is 167, i.e. it only needs 188px; 27px are spent there while the table grows wider. Header 'Example valid' / 'Error message' never wrap because they are never seen.
critique.cause: Total width is set by a generous pattern plus a surplus example column; the example column's 27px of slack and the pattern's last ~20px of slack both buy no line reduction, only scroll.

critique.good: Narrowest total (946px) and therefore the least scrolling; Field and Example sit at their exact no-split minimums (147, 188), and the error column at 180 still avoids mid-word breaks.
critique.problems: The pattern fragments are the least legible of the three — `[A-Za-z0-9])?(?:\.[A-Za-z0-` is split inside a character class and inside a lookahead, exactly the break the regex author would never choose, and account_email runs to 4 lines. Meanwhile rows are the *tallest* (849px), because the error column at 180 is at its floor and pushes the long date/VAT messages to 6 lines. So it pays both penalties: cramped regex and tall rows.
critique.cause: Pattern at 430 is below the ~470 threshold where regexes settle into 2–3 clean lines, and the error column is squeezed to 180 at the same time; the 60px saved against r2B were taken from the two columns that determine both readability and row height.

contrast.idea: A plausible 'just make it fit the box' compromise: everything sums to 359px, so nothing scrolls. But the Pattern column wraps every few characters into a vertical ribbon, the Field identifiers themselves break (account_email, effective_date), and headers stack word-by-word — the table is technically inside the frame and practically unreadable. Fitting the viewport is not the goal; keeping tokens intact is.

understanding.purpose: A developer/QA reference sheet: for each onboarding form field it gives the validation regex, a valid sample, and the message shown on failure — a lookup table read row by row while implementing or testing one field.
understanding.reading: Readers arrive knowing the field name (or scan the Field column as an index), then move right to the pattern, check it against the example, and read the error copy. Comparison happens within a row, not down a column, so each row must read as a single unit and the Field column must stay a stable anchor; the regex is the densest, most consulted content and the error text is the only true prose.
groups: col 1 Field is the row key and stands alone — it is the lookup handle and must remain visually distinct and unbroken
col 2 Pattern + col 3 Example valid form a spec pair: the rule and a value that satisfies it, read together and verified against each other
col 4 Error message is the outcome/consequence text, the only column of ordinary prose, and can wrap freely without losing meaning
keep_intact: field identifiers such as account_email, postal_code_us, currency_amount, eu_vat_id (no mid-word breaks)
regex anchors and atoms: ^, $, \d{7,14}, [A-Za-z0-9._!...], (?:-\d{4})? — break only at |, (, [, { boundaries, never inside a character class or quantifier
example values such as an email address or 2024-01-15 (break at @ or - at worst)
may_wrap: error-message sentences — natural prose, wraps at word spaces with no loss
long regex alternation/branch sequences — wrap between groups, not inside them
header labels 'Example valid' and 'Error message' over two lines

bad.why: Its 340px Pattern column is the only one that breaks regex tokens mid-word (2 mid-word splits), so a backslash class or quantifier is torn in two and the rule no longer reads as the code it is; and it buys nothing — the table is still the tallest at 919px with 6-line cells. Worst of both worlds: illegible code and maximum scrolling.

final.rationale: This is a reference table of machine-readable rules, so the Pattern column is the payload and its tokens must survive whole: a regex broken mid-token is not a wrapped word, it is a different string, which is why every zero-split design beats the narrower r1B despite costing more horizontal scroll. Among the zero-split options r3A is the only one that also minimises vertical cost — shortest table (733px), tallest cell 5 lines, and rows that stay compact enough to be read as units while scrolling back to the Field column. Field at 147px exactly fits its longest identifier (126px content) on one line, so the row anchor never wraps; the two prose columns can absorb generous wrapping because error messages are read after the rule, not compared across rows. Since the 360px box can only ever show Field plus the start of Pattern, the scroll is unavoidable and the honest move is to spend it on the column that cannot be abbreviated.

general: Never trade token integrity for viewport fit: code, regexes, IDs and file paths must wrap only at natural boundaries, even at the cost of horizontal scrolling.
Spend width where content is incompressible (code, identifiers), let prose columns absorb wrapping — they degrade gracefully, code does not.
The first column is the row anchor; size it so identifiers never wrap, then let everything else flex.
Extra width is only worth its scroll cost if it reduces row height or line count; r2A's 560px Pattern bought 726px of scroll and no height gain.
A short table is not automatically better, but among designs with equal token integrity, lower total height and fewer maximum lines wins.
specific: Field needs exactly ~147px here (126px longest identifier + 21px chrome); going below that starts breaking account_email and effective_date.
Pattern has 1074px of one-line content in a 360px viewport, so horizontal scrolling is a given; the only choice is whether tokens split (r1B) or not.
The Example valid column holds short regex snippets, not prose, so it also dislikes wrapping below ~170px.
Error message is the only true prose column and can safely run narrow; it is read after, not compared across rows.

final.tradeoffs: A reasonable designer could prefer r2B or r1C for the slightly wider Pattern (470px) and accept a 46–116px taller table, or argue r3C's 300px Pattern is the right compromise for less scrolling if 6-line cells are tolerable. Whether the reader is scrolling to compare patterns across rows (favours wider Pattern) or scanning field-by-field (favours shorter rows) is genuinely arguable.
final.uncertain: Without the rendered third and fourth columns it is hard to confirm how much the narrower Example valid column (188px) degrades; if those snippets must also stay on one line, the whole budget shifts and r2B's 215px becomes preferable. I also cannot verify whether the regex tokens at 465px wrap at operator boundaries or merely at spaces.
